etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ruby, rube, from Old French rubi, from Medieval Latin rubīnus.

definitions.definition: A clear, deep, red variety of corundum, valued as a precious stone.

quote.citation: 2012 March, Lee A. Groat, “Gemstones”, in American Scientist‎[1], volume 100, number 2, archived from the original on 14 June 2012, page 128:
quote.text: Although there are dozens of different types of gems, among the best known and most important are diamond, ruby and sapphire, emerald and other gem forms of the mineral beryl, chrysoberyl, tanzanite, tsavorite, topaz and jade.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iv]:
quote.text: When now I thinke you can behold such sights, / And keepe the naturall Rubie of your Cheekes, / When mine is blanch'd with feare.

quote.citation: 1720, Francis Nichols, Rudiments of Honour, page 296:
quote.text: Elgin. Topaz a Saltier and Chief Ruby, on a Canton Pearl a Lyon Rampant Saphyr, which last is their paternal Coat; and the Field Topaz, and Saltier, and Chief Ruby, was the Arms of King Robert the Bruce, they altering the Field from Pearl (as he bore it) to Topaz.

quote.citation: 1726, John Guillim, The Banner Display'd; Or, an Abridgment of Guillim, page 504:
quote.text: The Field is Ruby, on a Bend Topaz, three Martlets Diamond. [...] Checkie Topaz and Saphire, a Fesse within a Bordure Ruby, by the Name of Clifford.

quote.citation: 1754, John Lodge, The Peerage of Ireland; Or, a Genealogical History of the ..., page 71:
quote.text: (1) Pearl, a Cross, Ruby, with the Effigies of our Saviour thereon, Topaz, born in Memory of one of the Family's fighting against the Turks. (2) Topaz, a Chief Indented, Saphire. (3) Ruby, three covered Cups, Topaz [...]

definitions.definition: (uncountable, printing, UK, dated) The size of type between pearl and nonpareil, standardized as 5½-point.
A ruby hummer, a South American hummingbird, Clytolaema rubricauda.
(transitive, poetic) To make red; to redden.

quote.citation: 1725–1726, Homer, “Book 20”, in [William Broome, Elijah Fenton, Alexander Pope], transl., The Odyssey of Homer. […], London:  […]  Bernard Lintot, →OCLC:
quote.text: With sanguine drops the walls are rubied

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From the British 5½-point type size ruby (etymology 1), used for annotations in printed documents.

definitions.definition: (typography) A pronunciation guide written above or beside Chinese characters.
